tagline: As the “capital of capitals,” London keeps topping best-cities rankings. It is ranked #4 on Time Out's Best Cities 2026 list.
overview: London’s momentum has only grown. The Elizabeth line transformed cross-city travel — Heathrow to Tottenham Court Road in about 35 minutes — and visitor numbers have roared back to over 20 million international arrivals a year, keeping London the most-visited city in Europe.

The skyline story continues on the south bank of the Thames, where the restored Battersea Power Station has reopened as a shopping, dining and entertainment district complete with a chimney-top viewing lift. At the Olympic Park, the new East Bank cultural quarter keeps opening — V&A East and Sadler’s Wells East are already drawing crowds.

Theatre, museums and food remain world-beating: the West End sells out nightly, the British Museum and Tate Modern are still free, and the dining scene spans century-old chophouses to food halls across Borough Market, Spitalfields and Seven Dials.

For first-timers: book the Tower of London and West End shows ahead, tap in with contactless payment straight on the Tube (no Oyster card needed), and leave time for the neighborhoods — Greenwich, Notting Hill, Shoreditch and Hampstead Heath each feel like their own village.

funFacts.title: The City of London is tiny
funFacts.text: The huge city most people call London is officially Greater London. The City of London, its historic financial district, covers about one square mile and has fewer than 10,000 residents, making it one of the smallest cities in England.

funFacts.title: Technically a forest
funFacts.text: London has so many trees that it counts as an urban forest under a definition used by the United Nations. There are roughly as many trees in the city as there are people.

funFacts.title: Most of the Underground is above ground
funFacts.text: Despite its name, more than half of the London Underground network actually runs above ground. Londoners still call it the Tube.

funFacts.title: Big Ben isn't the tower
funFacts.text: Big Ben is the name of the great bell inside the clock tower at the Houses of Parliament. The tower itself has been called the Elizabeth Tower since 2012, so your selfie shows the tower, but you can still hear Big Ben chime.

funFacts.title: London isn't that rainy
funFacts.text: London has a reputation for rain, but it gets less rain each year than Rome, Miami or Sydney. Its weather is often grey and drizzly rather than wet.

funFacts.title: A capital of curry
funFacts.text: London has thousands of Indian, Bangladeshi and Pakistani restaurants, and Brick Lane is famous for its curry houses. Chicken tikka masala is often called one of Britain's national dishes.

funFacts.title: Don't expect fast traffic
funFacts.text: Cars in central London often move at an average of only about 7 to 8 miles per hour, not much faster than a horse and carriage. Walking or taking the Tube is usually quicker.

funFacts.title: The road where you drive on the right
funFacts.text: Everyone in Britain drives on the left, except on Savoy Court, the short road leading to the Savoy Hotel off the Strand. Drivers there are required to drive on the right.

funFacts.title: There's more than one London
funFacts.text: Many towns around the world share the name London, including London in Ontario, Canada, and several in the United States. Double-check your tickets so you end up in the original.

randomFacts: London has over 170 museums, including the British Museum, which is free to visit.
The London Underground, opened in 1863, is the oldest underground railway in the world.
Big Ben is the name of the bell, not the clock tower.
London has more than 8 million trees, making it one of the world's greenest cities.
The Tower of London houses the Crown Jewels, which are still used by the royal family.
The Romans founded London, which they called Londinium, almost 2,000 years ago.
More than 300 languages are spoken in London.
The London Eye is 135 metres tall and one of the largest observation wheels in Europe.
Buckingham Palace has 775 rooms, including 78 bathrooms.
London's red telephone boxes were designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott.
The River Thames is 215 miles long and flows through the heart of London.
London has four UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
The Shard is the tallest building in the UK at 310 metres.
Nearly half of London is green space, including Hyde Park and Regent's Park.
The British Library holds over 150 million items.

faq.a: London is in the United Kingdom, in Europe.

faq.q: What is the population of London?
faq.a: Greater London is home to about 9 million people, and the wider metro area to about 15.4 million.
London is famous for Big Ben, Buckingham Palace, the Tower of London, world-class free museums, and its West End theatres.
